title: Sarcoidosis and Mixed Connective Tissue Disease

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman has bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and a lymph-node biopsy showing non-caseating granulomas. Which definition does the source give?
opts: A chronic, multisystem, granulomatous immunological disorder with non-caseating granulomas on biopsy
An acute suppurative infection with neutrophilic abscesses
A vasculitic disorder of medium vessels
An eosinophilic infiltration of the lung and skin
questions.exp: Sarcoidosis is defined as a chronic, multisystem, granulomatous, immunological disorder; biopsy usually shows non-caseating granulomas. (Book p484)

questions.q: What exception to the non-caseating rule is printed?
opts: Caseation occurs only in the skin
Caseating granulomas can be seen in one-third of cases
Caseating granulomas never occur in sarcoidosis
Caseation is seen in every case
questions.exp: Biopsy usually shows non-caseating granulomas, but caseating granulomas can occur in one-third of cases. (Book p484)

questions.q: Which outcome spread is printed for sarcoidosis?
opts: About 5% resolve and 50% become chronic
All patients develop chronic fibrotic disease
About 50% resolve spontaneously, about 25% become chronic (mostly lung) and about 5% mortality attributed to ILD and infections
About 90% resolve and mortality is unknown
questions.exp: Outcome: 50% spontaneous resolution, 25% become chronic (mostly the lung is affected) and 5% mortality, attributed to interstitial lung disease and infections. (Book p484)

questions.q: A biopsy shows non-caseating granulomas and tuberculosis is being considered. Which other conditions does the source list as producing non-caseating granulomas?
opts: Only tuberculosis and leprosy
Only fungal infections
Only malignant conditions
30% of TB cases, lymphoma, berylliosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, Crohn disease and cat-scratch disease
questions.exp: Diseases that can have non-caseating granulomas: 30% of TB cases, lymphoma, berylliosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis (HP), Crohn's disease and cat-scratch disease. (Book p484)

questions.q: Which three items make up the ACR criteria for the diagnosis of sarcoidosis?
opts: A compatible clinical picture, histological non-caseating granulomas and exclusion of other causes
Raised ACE, a positive Mantoux test and hypercalcaemia
Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, fever and weight loss
A positive gallium scan, BAL lymphocytosis and skin anergy
questions.exp: ACR criteria: compatible clinical picture, histological non-caseating granulomas and exclusion of other causes. (Book p484)

questions.q: Which named syndromes head the acute and chronic branches of the classification?
opts: Acute: Sweet syndrome; chronic: Sjogren syndrome
Acute: Lofgren syndrome; chronic: Heerfordt syndrome
Acute: Heerfordt syndrome; chronic: Lofgren syndrome
Acute: Garland syndrome; chronic: Mikulicz syndrome
questions.exp: Classification: acute sarcoidosis is represented by Lofgren syndrome and chronic sarcoidosis by Heerfordt syndrome; hilar adenopathy is the important finding. (Book p484)

questions.q: A patient with sarcoidosis has lung, skin, eye and joint involvement and asks which organ is usually spared. Which ranking and spared organ does the source print?
opts: Eyes more than lung, with the liver spared
Joints most often, with the kidney spared
Lung (ILD) more than skin more than eyes more than joints, with only the testes spared
Skin more than lung more than eyes, with the spleen spared
questions.exp: Major manifestations: lung (ILD) more than skin more than eyes more than joints; multisystem manifestations include cardiac and renal disease, and the only organ spared is the testes. (Book p484)

questions.q: Which risk factors are listed for sarcoidosis?
opts: Smoking and asbestos exposure
Silica and vinyl chloride exposure
No risk factors are listed
Propionibacterium acnes infection and excessive firewood burning
questions.exp: Risk factors: Propionibacterium acnes infection and excessive firewood burning. (Book p484)

questions.sec: HLA Associations, Immune Paradox & Lofgren Syndrome
questions.q: A patient with Lofgren syndrome is HLA typed. Which association and prognosis does the source print?
opts: HLA-DRB1*03, associated with Lofgren syndrome and a good prognosis
HLA-DRB1*04, which is protective
HLA-DRB1*11, which marks CNS and cardiac disease
HLA-B27, which marks axial disease
questions.exp: HLA DRB1*03 is associated with Lofgren syndrome and a good prognosis. (Book p485)

questions.sec: HLA Associations, Immune Paradox & Lofgren Syndrome
questions.q: Which HLA types are printed as protective and as markers of poor prognosis respectively?
opts: Both mark severe disease
HLA-DRB1*04 is protective; HLA-DRB1*11 marks CNS and cardiac sarcoidosis with a bad prognosis
HLA-DRB1*11 is protective; HLA-DRB1*04 marks severe disease
Both are protective
questions.exp: HLA DRB1*04 has a protective role, while HLA DRB1*11 is associated with CNS and cardiac sarcoidosis, which carries a bad prognosis. (Book p485)

questions.sec: HLA Associations, Immune Paradox & Lofgren Syndrome
questions.q: Which HLA-disease pairs are repeated in the note on other diseases?
opts: DRB1*05 with SLE and Sjogren syndrome
No other associations are printed
DRB1*03 with SLE, Sjogren syndrome and dermatomyositis; DRB1*04 with APS and RA; DRB1*05 with scleroderma
DRB1*03 with scleroderma; DRB1*04 with SLE
questions.exp: The note repeats: HLA DRB1*03 with SLE, Sjogren syndrome and dermatomyositis; DRB1*04 with APS and RA; DRB1*05 with scleroderma. (Book p485)

questions.sec: HLA Associations, Immune Paradox & Lofgren Syndrome
questions.q: A patient with sarcoidosis has a negative Mantoux test despite previous BCG vaccination and has recurrent chest infections with lymphopenia. What does the source call this?
opts: Lymphocytosis with a strongly positive Mantoux test
Neutropenia with a false-positive Mantoux test
Eosinophilia with a normal immune response
Lymphopenia in the blood with a raised risk of infection, and a false-negative Mantoux test
questions.exp: Immune paradox/anergy: lymphopenia in blood leading to increased risk of infection, and a Mantoux test that is false negative because of low lymphocytes. (Book p485)

questions.sec: HLA Associations, Immune Paradox & Lofgren Syndrome
questions.q: Which observation is printed about HIV infection and sarcoidosis?
opts: HIV positivity lowers the lymphocyte count and lowers the risk of sarcoidosis
HIV positivity raises the risk of sarcoidosis
HIV has no relationship to sarcoidosis
Sarcoidosis protects against HIV infection
questions.exp: The note states HIV positivity leads to lymphopenia and a reduced risk of sarcoidosis. (Book p485)

questions.sec: HLA Associations, Immune Paradox & Lofgren Syndrome
questions.q: A young patient presents with tender pretibial nodules, ankle arthritis and bilateral hilar adenopathy. Which syndrome does the source name?
opts: Fever, night sweats and weight loss
Erythema nodosum, arthritis and hilar adenopathy
Uveitis, parotitis and facial nerve palsy
Lupus pernio, bone cysts and uveitis
questions.exp: Lofgren syndrome is drawn with erythema nodosum, arthritis and hilar adenopathy. (Book p485)

questions.sec: HLA Associations, Immune Paradox & Lofgren Syndrome
questions.q: How is the rash of sarcoidosis-associated erythema nodosum described?
opts: A vesicular rash on sun-exposed skin
A scarring panniculitis of the thighs
The 3 P's: painful, pretibial papules
The 3 P's: painless, pruritic plaques
questions.exp: Erythema nodosum in Lofgren syndrome is described with the 3 P's: painful, pretibial, papule. (Book p485)

questions.sec: HLA Associations, Immune Paradox & Lofgren Syndrome
questions.q: Which features are listed for the arthritis or tenosynovitis of acute sarcoidosis?
opts: Chronic, unilateral large-joint disease in the elderly
Erosive small-joint disease with nodules
Axial disease with sacroiliitis
Acute onset, ankle involvement, bilateral and symmetrical, occurring in young patients
questions.exp: Arthritis/tenosynovitis is acute, involves the ankle joint, is bilateral and symmetrical and is seen in the young. (Book p485)

questions.sec: Hilar Adenopathy, Heerfordt Syndrome & Chronic Sarcoidosis
questions.q: How does the source distinguish the erythema nodosum of Behcet disease?
opts: It has a fourth P: pigmentation, in addition to painful, pretibial papules
It is painless and non-pigmented
It is confined to the arms
It is identical to the sarcoid lesion
questions.exp: In Behcet's disease, erythema nodosum has 4 P's: painful, pretibial, papules with pigmentation. (Book p486)

questions.sec: Hilar Adenopathy, Heerfordt Syndrome & Chronic Sarcoidosis
questions.q: Which statement is printed about hilar adenopathy in sarcoidosis?
opts: It is a feature of tuberculosis, not sarcoidosis
It is the most consistent feature and is generally bilateral
It is rare and always unilateral
It occurs only in chronic disease
questions.exp: Hilar adenopathy is described as the most consistent feature and is generally bilateral, with right paratracheal and left hilar nodes shown. (Book p486)

questions.sec: Hilar Adenopathy, Heerfordt Syndrome & Chronic Sarcoidosis
questions.q: A patient with sarcoidosis has uveitis, bilateral facial nerve weakness and parotitis. Which syndrome and features does the source list?
opts: Lupus pernio, bone cysts and panuveitis
Hypercalcaemia, renal stones and pancytopenia
Uveitis, bilateral lower-motor-neuron seventh-nerve palsy and parotitis
Erythema nodosum, ankle arthritis and hilar adenopathy
questions.exp: Heerfordt-Waldenstrom syndrome: uveitis, bilateral LMN seventh-nerve palsy and parotitis. (Book p486)

questions.sec: Hilar Adenopathy, Heerfordt Syndrome & Chronic Sarcoidosis
questions.q: Which uveitis statements are printed for sarcoidosis?
opts: Only posterior uveitis occurs
Only episcleritis occurs
The eye is never involved in sarcoidosis
Any type or compartment can be involved, acute anterior uveitis is more common and uveitis is the most common ocular manifestation
questions.exp: Uveitis: any type or compartment, acute anterior uveitis more common, and the most common ocular manifestation of sarcoid. (Book p486)

questions.sec: Hilar Adenopathy, Heerfordt Syndrome & Chronic Sarcoidosis
questions.q: A patient with sarcoidosis develops bilateral lower-motor-neuron facial weakness. What does the source call this manifestation?
opts: Bilateral lower-motor-neuron seventh-nerve palsy
Aseptic meningitis
Peripheral sensorimotor neuropathy
Cerebellar ataxia
questions.exp: Bilateral LMN seventh-nerve palsy is the most common neurological manifestation in sarcoid; the note pairs it with Guillain-Barre syndrome as its main differential. (Book p486)

questions.sec: Hilar Adenopathy, Heerfordt Syndrome & Chronic Sarcoidosis
questions.q: What is the clinical paradox of chronic pulmonary sarcoidosis?
opts: Nodes and parenchyma are unrelated to the disease stage
As the lung disease worsens, the nodal enlargement regresses, which helps identify chronicity
Nodes enlarge in proportion to the parenchymal disease
Nodes calcify while the parenchyma remains normal
questions.exp: Clinical paradox: it helps identify chronicity, because as the lung disease worsens the nodal enlargement regresses. (Book p486)

questions.sec: Hilar Adenopathy, Heerfordt Syndrome & Chronic Sarcoidosis
questions.q: Serial imaging shows hilar nodes regressing as parenchymal infiltrates appear, and later fibrosis. How does the source stage chronic sarcoidosis?
opts: There are only two stages
Staging is based on symptoms, not imaging
Stage 1 bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy; stage 2 nodal enlargement with parenchymal disease; stage 3 parenchymal disease only; stage 4 fibrosis
Stage 1 fibrosis; stage 2 nodes; stage 3 infiltrates; stage 4 calcification
questions.exp: Stages: 1 bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with nodal enlargement only, 2 nodal enlargement plus parenchymal disease (node size starts to fall as infiltrate rises), 3 parenchymal disease only, 4 fibrosis. (Book p486)

questions.q: Which features are printed for the fibrosis pattern of sarcoidosis?
opts: Lower-lobe honeycombing with pleural plaques
Diffuse cystic change with pneumothorax
Cavitation with fungal balls
Thickening of the bronchovascular bundles with upper-lobe traction bronchiectasis
questions.exp: Fibrosis pattern: thickening of bronchovascular bundles and traction bronchiectasis of the upper lobe; upper-lobe fibrosis is also listed for ankylosing spondylitis and sarcoidosis. (Book p487)

questions.q: A patient has violaceous indurated plaques over the central face that respond poorly to treatment. How does the source describe this lesion?
opts: Violaceous or erythematous, indurated infiltrative plaques on the central face that respond poorly to treatment
A painless pretibial nodule that resolves spontaneously
A photosensitive malar rash sparing the nasolabial fold
A pruritic papular rash over the knuckles
questions.exp: Lupus pernio: violaceous or erythematous, indurated, infiltrative plaques on the central face that are less responsive to treatment; bone changes (lytic or cystic) are also associated. (Book p487)

questions.q: Which eye manifestation is described as the most common in chronic sarcoidosis?
opts: Keratoconjunctivitis sicca
Chronic bilateral panuveitis
Acute anterior uveitis
Episcleritis
questions.exp: Eye involvement: chronic bilateral panuveitis is the most common manifestation. (Book p487)

questions.q: Which feature is listed as UNLIKELY in sarcoidosis?
opts: Upper-lobe fibrosis
Non-caseating granulomas
Pleural involvement
Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy
questions.exp: Features unlikely of sarcoidosis: pleural involvement and a UIP-like pattern with honeycombing and parenchymal destruction in the lung; episcleritis, scleritis and sicca in the eye. (Book p487)

questions.q: Which ocular findings are listed as unlikely in sarcoidosis?
opts: Anterior uveitis and vitritis
Retinal vasculitis and choroidal granulomas
Optic nerve granulomas
Episcleritis, scleritis and sicca
questions.exp: The note lists episcleritis, scleritis and sicca as ocular features unlikely of sarcoidosis. (Book p487)

questions.q: Which endocrine abnormality is listed for sarcoidosis?
opts: Hypercalcaemia
Hypocalcaemia with tetany
Hypothyroidism
Adrenal insufficiency
questions.exp: Endocrine manifestation: hypercalcaemia. (Book p488)

questions.q: A patient with sarcoidosis develops polyuria and polydipsia from a pituitary mass. Which neurological manifestations does the source list?
opts: Parkinsonian rigidity with tremor
Bilateral LMN seventh-nerve palsy, pituitary mass with stalk effect causing central diabetes insipidus, basilar meningitis and acute transverse myelitis
Guillain-Barre syndrome with albuminocytological dissociation
Multiple sclerosis with periventricular plaques
questions.exp: CNS: bilateral LMN seventh-nerve palsy (most common), neurosarcoidosis with a pituitary mass causing stalk effect and central diabetes insipidus, basilar meningitis and acute transverse myelitis. (Book p488)

questions.q: Which cardiac manifestations are listed?
opts: Aortic stenosis with regurgitation
Infective endocarditis of native valves
Dilated cardiomyopathy more than restrictive cardiomyopathy, with AV block
Constrictive pericarditis with tamponade
questions.exp: CVS: dilated cardiomyopathy more than restrictive cardiomyopathy, and AV blocks. (Book p488)

questions.q: Which haematological manifestation is printed for sarcoidosis?
opts: Isolated lymphocytosis without cytopenias
Polycythaemia with thrombocytosis
Haemolytic anaemia with jaundice
Pancytopenia with splenomegaly
questions.exp: Hematology: pancytopenia with splenomegaly. (Book p488)

questions.q: A patient with sarcoidosis has renal impairment and hypercalcaemia. Which renal manifestations does the source print?
opts: AKI from hypercalcaemia-induced pre-renal failure, CKD from chronic tubulointerstitial disease, and rare glomerular membranous nephropathy
Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with crescents
Immune-complex lupus nephritis
Analgesic nephropathy
questions.exp: Renal: AKI is hypercalcaemia-induced pre-renal failure, CKD is chronic tubulointerstitial disease (CTID) and the glomerulus is rarely affected, with membranous nephropathy. (Book p488)

questions.q: Which rheumatological disorders are listed as causes of chronic tubulointerstitial disease?
opts: Ankylosing spondylitis and reactive arthritis
Sjogren syndrome, IgG4-related disease and sarcoidosis
SLE, systemic sclerosis and dermatomyositis
Rheumatoid arthritis, gout and pseudogout
questions.exp: The note lists rheumatological disorders causing CTID as Sjogren's syndrome, IgG4-related disease and sarcoidosis. (Book p488)

questions.q: Which imaging investigations and their roles are printed?
opts: CT pulmonary angiography and echocardiography
MRI of the brain and nerve-conduction studies
Gallium-67 scintigraphy with the panda sign, and PET scanning to identify the node to biopsy
Plain radiography alone and ventilation-perfusion scanning
questions.exp: Investigations: gallium-67 scintigraphy (panda sign) and PET scan, which is the investigation of choice to identify nodes to take a biopsy from. (Book p488)

questions.q: Which blood markers are listed, and what does a normal value of the first marker imply?
opts: C-reactive protein and ESR; a normal CRP rules out sarcoidosis
Calcium and phosphate; normal calcium rules out sarcoidosis
Ferritin and transferrin saturation; normal ferritin rules out sarcoidosis
Angiotensin-converting enzyme and soluble interleukin-2 receptor; a normal ACE can rule out sarcoidosis
questions.exp: Blood markers: angiotensin-converting enzyme (if normal, sarcoidosis can be ruled out) and soluble interleukin-2 (sIL-2) receptor. (Book p488)

questions.q: Bronchoalveolar lavage is performed in a patient with suspected sarcoidosis. Which lavage finding does the source list?
opts: A raised CD4/CD8 ratio above the printed cut-off
A predominance of CD8-positive lymphocytes
Neutrophil-predominant cellularity
Eosinophils above 25% of the cell count
questions.exp: Bronchoalveolar lavage is listed with a raised CD4/CD8 ratio above the cut-off printed on the page. (Book p488)

questions.q: How is acute sarcoidosis managed according to the printed treatment block?
opts: Anti-TNF therapy
No treatment is required
Immediate high-dose steroid
Methotrexate monotherapy
questions.exp: Treatment: acute sarcoidosis requires no treatment; chronic disease is treated in steps. (Book p489)

questions.q: Which stepwise regimen is printed for chronic sarcoidosis?
opts: First line azathioprine; second line anti-TNF; third line steroids
Steroids at every step with no steroid-sparing agents
First line steroids; second line methotrexate or azathioprine; third line anti-TNF-alpha with adalimumab
First line methotrexate; second line steroids; third line cyclophosphamide
questions.exp: Chronic: first line steroids, second line methotrexate and azathioprine, third line anti-TNF-alpha (adalimumab). (Book p489)

questions.q: What is the therapeutic paradox described on this page?
opts: Steroids cure sarcoidosis but cause reactivation of tuberculosis
Anti-TNF therapy prevents all skin lesions of sarcoidosis
Methotrexate worsens uveitis in sarcoidosis
Patients treated with TNF-alpha blockade can develop sarcoid-like skin lesions that disappear on reducing the dose
questions.exp: Therapeutic paradox: in a patient treated with TNF-alpha (adalimumab), skin lesions similar to sarcoidosis can appear, and they disappear on reducing the dose. (Book p489)

questions.q: How is an overlap syndrome defined on this page?
opts: Features of at least two of the six autoimmune systemic connective-tissue diseases
Features of all six connective-tissue diseases at once
A single connective-tissue disease with extra-articular features
Any positive autoantibody with a compatible symptom
questions.exp: Overlap syndrome: features of two or more out of the six autoimmune systemic connective tissue diseases. (Book p489)

questions.q: Which diseases are listed in the overlap group, and which is most common?
opts: Only the inflammatory muscle diseases
Sjogren syndrome (most common, usually with anti-Ro), SLE, polymyositis, dermatomyositis, systemic sclerosis and rheumatoid arthritis
Only SLE and systemic sclerosis
Only rheumatoid arthritis and Sjogren syndrome
questions.exp: The overlap list is Sjogren syndrome (most common, most having anti-Ro antibody), SLE, polymyositis, dermatomyositis, systemic sclerosis and rheumatoid arthritis. (Book p489)

questions.q: How is the treatment of an overlap syndrome chosen?
opts: It is always antimalarial monotherapy
No treatment is possible
It is based on the predominant disease
It is always high-dose cyclophosphamide
questions.exp: The source states that treatment is based on the predominant disease in the overlap. (Book p489)

questions.q: How is undifferentiated connective-tissue disease defined?
opts: Patients with a negative autoantibody panel and no symptoms
Patients with two established connective-tissue diseases
Patients with drug-induced autoantibodies
Patients with some features of a connective-tissue disease who do not fulfil criteria for classification as a specific disease
questions.exp: Undifferentiated CTD: patients presenting with some features of CTD who do not fulfil the criteria to be classified under a disease. (Book p489)

questions.q: A middle-aged woman has Raynaud phenomenon, swollen hands, myositis and a very high titre anti-U1 RNP. How does the source introduce this disease?
opts: As a specific type of overlap syndrome presenting with unique features in middle-aged females
As a form of systemic lupus erythematosus with nephritis
As a vasculitic disorder of medium vessels
As a granulomatous disease of the lung
questions.exp: MCTD is introduced as a specific type of overlap syndrome, with patients presenting unique features, in middle-aged females (female:male about 15:1). (Book p489)

questions.q: Serology is requested in a patient with suspected mixed connective-tissue disease. Which profile does the source print?
opts: ANA positive with a centromere pattern and anti-centromere antibody
ANA positive in 100% with a coarse speckled pattern and a positive anti-U1 RNP antibody
ANA negative with a positive anti-Jo-1 antibody
ANA positive with a homogeneous pattern and anti-dsDNA
questions.exp: Serology: ANA positive in 100% with a coarse speckled pattern and anti-U1 RNP antibody positive. (Book p489)

questions.q: A middle-aged woman with anti-U1 RNP positivity presents with cold-induced digital colour change. Which manifestation does the source call most common?
opts: CNS vasculitis
Lupus pernio
Raynaud's phenomenon
Nephritis
questions.exp: Clinical features: Raynaud's phenomenon is the most common manifestation, followed by oedema of hands, nail pitting, acrosclerosis, myositis and erosive synovitis. (Book p490)

questions.q: How is acrosclerosis defined on this page?
opts: Isolated sclerodactyly without Raynaud's phenomenon
Calcification of the digital arteries
Ulceration of the fingertips alone
Raynaud's phenomenon combined with MCTD and systemic-sclerosis features of the hand
questions.exp: Acrosclerosis is defined as Raynaud's phenomenon plus MCTD plus the systemic-sclerosis features of the hand. (Book p490)

questions.q: Which systems are usually spared in MCTD according to the clinical-features list?
opts: The CNS and the renal system
The skin and joints
The lungs and heart
The gastrointestinal tract and liver
questions.exp: Clinical features note that the CNS and renal system are usually spared in MCTD. (Book p490)

questions.q: Which HLA association is printed for MCTD?
opts: HLA-DQ8
HLA-DRB1*04
HLA-DRB1*03
HLA-B27
questions.exp: HLA association for MCTD: HLA DRB1*04. (Book p490)

questions.q: Which complications and outcome figures are printed for MCTD?
opts: Cardiac involvement occurs in 20% and is the leading cause of death
There are no recognised complications
ILD is the most common complication; about 20% evolve into limited systemic sclerosis with pulmonary artery hypertension, the most common cause of death
Nephritis is the most common complication and it causes most deaths
questions.exp: Complications: ILD is the most common, and about 20% evolve into limited SSc with pulmonary artery hypertension, which is the most common cause of death. (Book p490)

questions.q: Which capillaroscopy appearances are shown for Raynaud's phenomenon in MCTD?
opts: Only a completely normal capillary pattern
Only giant capillaries with thrombosis
Capillary dropout in every field
Normal, dilated, tortuous, bushy and meandering capillaries with microhaemorrhage
questions.exp: The capillaroscopy panel in RP shows normal, dilated, tortuous, bushy and meandering capillaries with microhaemorrhage. (Book p490)

units.title: 1. Sarcoidosis Definition, ACR Criteria & Classification
units.guide:
The definition pairs the granuloma type with its recognised exceptions.
Outcome, ACR diagnostic criteria and the acute-versus-chronic classification follow.
Organ ranking and risk factors close the introductory survey.

units.title: 2. HLA Associations, Immune Paradox & Lofgren Syndrome
units.sec: HLA Associations, Immune Paradox & Lofgren Syndrome
units.guide:
HLA associations are split into prognosis, protection and severe-organ disease.
The immune-paradox block explains anergy and the false-negative Mantoux test.
Lofgren syndrome then opens acute sarcoidosis with its classic triad.

units.title: 3. Hilar Adenopathy, Heerfordt Syndrome & Chronic Sarcoidosis
units.sec: Hilar Adenopathy, Heerfordt Syndrome & Chronic Sarcoidosis
units.guide:
The erythema-nodosum comparison separates sarcoidosis from Behcet disease.
Heerfordt syndrome is then defined by its ocular, facial-nerve and salivary features.
Chronic disease is staged by the paradoxical relationship between nodes and parenchyma.

units.title: 4. Fibrosis, Skin & Eye Involvement
units.guide:
The fibrosis pattern is defined by bronchovascular thickening and upper-lobe traction.
Lupus pernio is then characterised by site, texture and treatment response.
A note lists the features that make sarcoidosis unlikely.

units.title: 5. Multisystem Manifestations & Investigations
units.guide:
Endocrine, neurological, cardiac, haematological and renal disease are listed organ by organ.
A note groups the rheumatological causes of chronic tubulointerstitial disease.
Imaging, blood markers and BAL close the investigation sequence.

units.title: 6. Treatment, Therapeutic Paradox & Overlap Syndromes
units.guide:
Treatment is stratified by acuteness, with observation for acute disease.
The therapeutic paradox reconciles tumour-necrosis-factor blockade with sarcoid-like lesions.
Overlap syndromes and undifferentiated connective-tissue disease are then defined.

units.title: 7. MCTD: Serology, Clinical Features & Complications
units.guide:
Mixed connective-tissue disease is introduced as a specific type of overlap syndrome.
Serology is dominated by a universal ANA pattern and anti-U1 RNP positivity.
Clinical features and complications are then contrasted with systemic sclerosis.
